title: Book Corner
strapline: A cosy nest of stories where children fall in love with books — and stay long enough to make them their own.
intent: Children build a deep bank of core stories they know inside out — well enough to join in, retell and argue about the ending.
Children learn how books work: front cover, right way up, page by page, print carries the meaning.
Children meet rich vocabulary in context and carry it out into their play.
Children discover that books are somewhere to go — a place to rest, wonder and return to favourites again and again.
Children begin to see themselves as readers: choosing, holding and 'reading' books to friends, teddies and themselves.
implementation: Keep a small set of core books constantly available and re-read them until children can say the next line before you do — depth beats novelty.
Display books face-out at child height, with cushions and soft light that say 'stay a while' rather than 'choose and go'.
Read with relish: voices, pauses, dramatic page turns — then hand over the refrains ('...you can't catch me!') and wait.
Run a finger under the title now and then and name the parts in passing: cover, author, page — little and often, never a lesson.
Leave story props and soft toys from core books in the corner so retelling can start without an adult.
Notice what a child brings to the story ('my dog!') and follow it — the link to their own life is the hook.
Refresh a small guest shelf with the season, current interests and books showing many kinds of families and homes — but never rotate the core set away.
key_questions: What do you think will happen when we turn the page?
Where shall we start reading — how do you know?
Which bit shall we read again? Why that bit?
What would you have done if you were the fox?
Does this remind you of anything that's happened to you?

impact.text: Children fetch a favourite book unprompted, hold it the right way up and turn pages one at a time.
Children join in with repeated refrains and shout the missing word before the adult reads it.
Children point at pictures, name what they see and connect it to their own lives — 'that's like my nanny's cat'.
Children talk about the story as it unfolds — what's happening, what might happen next, which bit they liked.
Children notice print around the corner — the title, their name card on the borrowing pocket, familiar labels.
Children retell core stories with a beginning, middle and end, using props or puppets, and invent cheeky variations.
Children 'read' books aloud to a friend or teddy from pictures and memory, using their story voice.
Children use story words in their own talk and play days later — 'enormous', 'trudged', 'terrible tusks'.

enhancements: A story basket per core book — puppets, real objects (a tin of beans for the shopping story, a wooden spoon, three bowls) for independent retelling.
A 'story vote' — two book covers on the easel and name cards to post under today's group-time choice.
A borrowing pocket wall so children take a core book home and bring back what their family thought.
Author of the fortnight — cluster three books by one author and hunt for what's the same in the pictures.
A story stage: small screen, felt pieces and character cut-outs next to the corner for performing endings — including the wrong ones.
A listening spot with a story recorded by a familiar voice — a key person, or a parent reading in a home language.
A repair kit (tape, 'book hospital' box) so children learn that books are cared for, not thrown.

playing_exploring: Children choose books freely and revisit favourites again and again, showing a 'can do' relationship with reading.
Story props invite children to step inside a book and play it out their own way.
active_learning: Children persist through a whole book, holding the thread of a story to its end.
Anticipating the refrain and being right is its own reward — you can see the satisfaction land.
creating_thinking: Children make links between stories and their own lives, and between one story and another.
Inventing new endings and arguing about them is early critical thinking at its best.
